state.misconception_label: Believes if you changed all values by the same proportion the range would not change

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: Tom and Katie are discussing the \( 5 \) plants with these heights: \( 24 \mathrm{~cm}, 17 \mathrm{~cm}, 42 \mathrm{~cm}, 26 \mathrm{~cm}, 13 \mathrm{~cm} \) Tom says if all the plants were cut in half, the range wouldn't change. Katie says if all the plants grew by \( 3 \mathrm{~cm} \) each, the range wouldn't change. Who do you agree with? I got Only
Tom because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Why do you think changing all the plants by the same proportion would not affect the range? Can you think of a scenario where changing all the heights by the same proportion would change the range?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I guess I thought that if you cut everything in half, the difference between the tallest and shortest plants would stay the same. But now I'm not sure. If you change all the heights by the same amount, like adding \(3 \mathrm{~cm}\), wouldn't that just move everything up and keep the range the same too? Can you explain how that works?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Can you think about how changing all the heights by the same amount might affect the difference between the tallest and shortest plants? Think about the concept of range and how it relates to the individual plant heights.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Okay, I think I get what you're saying. If I add \(3 \mathrm{~cm}\) to all the plants, the tallest plant will still be the tallest and the shortest will still be the shortest, so the range would stay the same. But if I cut everything in half, I guess the difference between the tallest and shortest plants would still be the same too, right? I'm still a bit confused about how changing by a proportion works. Can you help me understand that better?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher asks questions to promote reasoning but fails to address the specific misconception about proportional change, and by Turn 4 the student remains confused about the key distinction between additive and multiplicative changes, showing no real progress toward correcting the original error.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently uses probing questions to guide the student's thinking and never directly provides the answer, though they could have been more effective by using a concrete counterexample to expose the student's flawed reasoning about proportional changes.
